title: Manufacturing Abdominal Aorta Hydrogel Tissue-Mimicking Phantoms for Ultrasound Elastography Validation
protocol: Download STL Models from the NIH 3D Print Exchange.
Navigate to the NIH 3D Print Exchange (3dprint.nih.gov).
Type "Simulated Aneurysmal Aortic Phantom Mold" in the search entry and hit enter.
Find and click on the model "3DPX-009210".
Click the download button and select the Simulated Aneurysmal Aortic Phantom Mold.zip file to download it.
Unzip the downloaded file.
Store the resulting STL files (InnerDistSTL.stl, InnerProxSTL.stl, OuterAntSTL.stl, OuterPostSTL.stl, BackgroundMoldSTL.stl and SampleMoldSTL.stl) on the computer used for 3D printing.
Connect to the 3D printer using the printer interface software.
Import the STL file OuterAntSTL.stl into the 3D printing software.
Orient the mold part by clicking the Rotate menu and then clicking the X, Y, or Z buttons in the Edit button section of the software.
Save the oriented mold part.
Print the mold part using polylactic acid (PLA) plastic filament on a single extruder.
Import the STL file SampleMoldSTL.stl into the 3D printing software.
Select the Edit button.
In the Rotate menu, click the X, Y, or Z buttons to align the part such that the inside of the mold is facing up from the print bed.
Click the Save button.
Click the Print button and print the mold part using PLA plastic filament on a single extruder.
Do not print this part with the support structure.
Print 3 or more sample molds.
Import the STL file BackgroundMoldSTL.stl into the 3D printing software.
Select the Edit button.
In the Rotate menu, click the X, Y, or Z buttons to align the part such that the bottom of the mold is facing the print bed.
Click the Save button.
Click the Print button and print the mold part using PLA plastic filament on a single extruder.
Do not print this part with the support structure.
Import the STL file InnerDistSTL.stl into the 3D printing software.
Select the Edit button.
In the Rotate menu, click the X, Y, or Z buttons to align the part such that the long axis is perpendicular to the print bed and bifurcation registration pins are facing the print bed.
Click the Save button.
Click the Print button and print the mold part using polyvinyl acid (PVA) plastic filament on a single extruder.
Remove any support material from the 3D printed parts of Steps 2.1-2.7.
Mix 22.2 g of PVA-c powder in 200 mL of tap water (10% by mass) in a glass beaker.
Microwave the solution to a boil and stir until all of the PVA powder is dissolved and the solution appears translucent.
Suspend 0.4 g of calcium carbonate powder in 10 mL of water.
Add the suspension to the solution from Step 2.1.
Mix thoroughly.
Cover the solution and allow it to cool to room temperature.
Mix 17.6 g of PVA-c powder in 100 mL of tap water.
Microwave the solution to a boil and stir until all the PVA powder is dissolved and the solution appears translucent.
Suspend 0.4 g of calcium carbonate powder in 5 mL of water.
Add the suspension to the solution from Step 2.3.
Mix thoroughly.
Cover the solution and allow it to cool to room temperature.
Mix 183.7 g of PVA-c powder in 3.5 L of tap water.
Bring the solution to a boil and stir until all the PVA powder is dissolved and the solution appears translucent.
Suspend 7.4 g of calcium carbonate powder in 10 mL of water.
Add the suspension to the solution from Step 2.5.
Mix thoroughly.
Cover the solution and allow it to cool to room temperature.
Attach approximately 100 mm of flexible tubing to the injection port of the outer lumen mold.
Connect a stopcock with syringe connections to the opposite end of the tubing.
Align the registration pins of the inner lumen mold.
Adhere the bulging vessel part of the inner lumen mold to the straight vessel part using deformable wax.
Apply a spray-on flexible rubber coating to the aneurysmal end of the inner lumen mold in a well-ventilated area.
With the larger side of the aneurysmal part facing down, fill the bulge with 15 mL of the solution from Steps 3.3-3.4.
Place the assembled inner mold parts into the front outer mold part.
Hold the inner lumen part in place using rubber bands.
Freeze the mold assembly in a -20 °C freezer for 12 hours.
Remove the mold assembly from the freezer without letting it thaw.
Apply a generous amount of deformable wax to the back surface of a printed sample mold.
Clamp the sample mold to a flat plastic sheet cut to approximately 100 mm by 60 mm by 10 mm.
Fill the space between the mold and the plastic sheet with the same PVA solution used previously.
Freeze the sample mold in a freezer at -20 °C.
Assemble and clamp together the entire vessel mold in the orientation shown.
Line the seams of the outer lumen molds using deformable wax to prevent leaks.
Fill a 60 mL syringe with the PVA-c solution prepared earlier.
Inject the PVA-c solution into the mold assembly, avoiding air bubbles.
Patch leaky areas with deformable wax if any leaks occur during the injection.
Repeat syringe injections until the PVA-c solution fills the mold.
Tap the mold gently every 10 min for 30 min to allow air bubbles to rise.
Top off the mold with additional PVA-c solution as needed.
Freeze the entire mold assembly for 12 hours.
Allow the mold assembly to thaw at room temperature for 12 hours.
Assemble and clamp another sample mold and flat plastic sheet.
Fill the space between the mold and the plastic sheet with PVA solution.
Freeze and thaw the sample mold in the same freezer as the vessel mold.
Repeat freeze/thaw cycles four more times, totaling five 24-hour cycles.
Remove PVA-c testing samples from their molds after the fifth cycle.
Trim excess cryogel from the samples.
Store samples in a sealed container of a 5% by volume bleach/water solution at room temperature.
Remove the PVA-c vessel from the outer lumen mold.
Separate the straight vessel part of the inner lumen mold from the aneurysmal part.
Carefully remove the separated parts from the PVA-c vessel.
Cut the registration spacers from the bifurcated end of the aneurysmal part of the inner lumen mold to expose the printed PVA filament.
Place the exposed phantom in a water bath at room temperature to dissolve the PVA aneurysmal part.
Fill the background mold with approximately 3.3 L of the PVA-c solution made previously.
Freeze the background mold for 12 hours at -20 °C.
Remove the frozen background mold from the freezer and allow it to thaw at room temperature for 12 hours.
Repeat the freeze/thaw cycles for a total of two cycles.
Fill a sample mold assembly with the same PVA-c solution used in Step 4.13.
Put the sample mold through the same freeze/thaw cycles as the background mold.
After the second thaw cycle, remove the background sample and background phantom from their molds.
Store the background sample and phantom in a sealed container of a 5% by volume bleach/water solution at room temperature.
Place the vessel phantom and background phantom into a large water bath.
Attach the larger vessel end to the output of the hemodynamic water pump using tubing clamps.
Place the vessel phantom inside the background phantom.
Attach the bifurcated ends of the vessel phantom to the inlet of the hemodynamic pump using tubing clamps.
Insert a solid-state pressure sensor catheter into the system near the inlet of the hemodynamic pump.
Run the hemodynamic pump to maintain pressures between 0 kPa and 7.5 kPa.

Use an ultrasound (US) system with a convex transducer having a center frequency of approximately 5 MHz to collect US images of the background and vessel phantoms in cross-section at the location of the maximum vessel diameter.
Record pressure data using a digital acquisition system.
Use a non-rigid image registration-based technique to obtain displacement estimations.
Calculate the 2D strain tensor field from the measurements of the 2D displacement field.
Evaluate the symmetric part of the gradient of the displacement field for the strain tensor calculation.
Calculate the maximum principal strain as the maximum principal component of the strain tensor field.
Determine the frame of the principal strain at the peak pressure.
Divide this strain tensor field by the difference in the maximum and minimum catheter-measured pressures, or the pulse pressure, to spatially resolve the pressure-normalized principle strain.
